fieldFixes.normativeTextNote: Read in full on 2026-09-23: the IEEE Xplore PDF (50 pages; printed page numbers run to 48), served free through the IEEE GET Program at https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stampPDF/getPDF.jsp?tp=&arnumber=11360682&ref=. Clauses 1-5 are normative; cl. 1.4 defines 'shall' as mandatory, 'should' as recommended and 'may' as permitted. The Introduction states that it 'is not part of' the standard, and cl. 6 says 'All annex contents are to be considered informative': Annex A (draft terms with sample code — the SD-BASE and PDC agreement codes, a bitwise 'CONTRACT ZONE' encoding, an HTTP-header example, RDF/Turtle, JSON, JSON-LD, RSS and Pickle samples), Annex B (two use cases), Annex C (abbreviated designations, pointing to Customer Commons), Annex D (ISO 23903 interoperability) and Annex E (bibliography). No agreement is named in clauses 1-5: the agreement codes, the counter-offer walk-through and the DPV/ODRL recommendation are all in informative Annex A. The text's own cross-references are imperfect: cl. 6 swaps Annexes C and D, cl. 5.5 points to Annex E for interoperability, and Table A.1's legend contradicts the sentence before it about what its symbols mean.

fieldFixes.abstractNote: Verbatim from the IEEE SA standard page and from the abstract page of the published PDF. The explicit AI-agent language appears in the final text, but only here: clauses 1-5 never use the word 'AI'. The abstract is front matter, and its 'shall' sentences summarise cl. 4-5, with two differences. 'Any protocol that serves the purpose' appears in no numbered clause (cl. 1.3 says operation 'depends on the Internet Protocol Suite, especially TCP/IP, and HTTP'). fieldFixes.plainSummary: The default: the site or service provides what the person came for and does not share information about them with other parties. fieldFixes.summary: The standard requires terms and contracts to be kept and displayed on a public website by 'a neutral nonprofit entity or neutral party that is not economically dependent on terms use' (cl. 4.2; the abstract says 'an independent and neutral non-business entity'). It names no keeper in its normative clauses. Customer Commons, a US 501(c)(3) spun out of ProjectVRM, appears only in informative notes and annexes, as the home of the current sample terms. In practice Customer Commons names and hosts the MyTerms agreements on the Creative Commons model, and a European MyTerms Alliance is to contribute regional variants.

issues: Contradicted in part. 'The standard deliberately leaves the record format, storage and protocol open' repeats the MyTerms FAQ ('an option left open by the MyTerms standard'), but the normative text fixes the record's content and properties. Cl. 5.2.4: the recorder 'shall record the agreement and handshake terms, date, time stamp, and pseudonymous or explicit identifiers, containing a unique contract ID', and 'shall record rejected agreements'. Cl. 5.4.4: 'The exact time, date, and location shall be recorded' and 'Identical, immutable copies ... shall be recorded in each party’s data store'. Cl. 5.2.2: copies are delivered to both parties 'immediately upon agreement signing'. Cl. 5.2.3: the handshake carries a unique contract identifier. What is left open is the medium ('Storage shall be substitutable', with data portability) and the concrete serialisation. Signing is required, but its method is 'any standard method agreed upon' (cl. 5.4.2). The protocol point comes from the abstract only (see any-protocol).

Informative Annex A says 'the recording of contracts following the agreement between the two agents is also not in scope' (FOUND) and points to DPV and ODRL. That sits oddly with normative cl. 5.2.4 and 5.4.4, which do set recording requirements, and as annex text it cannot override them.

fieldFixes.summary: If both parties agree, both agents sign electronically, 'using any standard method agreed upon for that purpose' (cl. 5.4.2). Digital copies go to both parties immediately (cl. 5.2.2), and each keeps an identical, immutable copy in its own data store for later access, audit or dispute (cl. 5.4.4). The standard sets the record's minimum content: the agreement and handshake terms, date, time stamp, pseudonymous or explicit identifiers and a unique contract ID (cl. 5.2.4), plus the exact time, date and location (cl. 5.4.4). A refusal must be recorded too. What it leaves open is the file format and the storage medium ('Storage shall be substitutable', with data portability). The MyTerms FAQ's 'option left open' is therefore true of format and storage, not of content. Doc Searls's January 2026 'MyTerms Agreement Record' (MAR) sketch is his own proposal, not part of the standard.

issues: 'Any protocol that serves the purpose' is abstract wording (front matter). No numbered clause repeats it. The normative text says operation 'depends on the Internet Protocol Suite, especially TCP/IP, and HTTP' (cl. 1.3) and leaves the signing method to the parties (cl. 5.4.2). 'The standard does not specify the technology' remains broadly right, but it should rest on the abstract plus cl. 1.3, not on the abstract alone.
The FAQ's browser-header idea has a counterpart in the standard only as an informative example: Annex A.2 shows an HTTP request carrying 'MRPAZ-' and 'MTPAZ-' header fields. It is not a requirement.

fieldFixes.summary: The abstract says agents for both parties 'shall engage using any protocol that serves the purpose'. The numbered clauses name no signalling protocol: they say only that operation 'depends on the Internet Protocol Suite, especially TCP/IP, and HTTP' (cl. 1.3), and let the agents sign 'using any standard method agreed upon' (cl. 5.4.2). An HTTP-header encoding appears only as an informative example (Annex A.2). The proponents' early sketches centre on browser and web-server plug-ins (the FAQ suggests signalling through browser headers on the model of Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control), and they expect AI to play a larger part as products develop. MyData Global (August 2026) lists apps, digital wallets and agentic AI among possible agents and says personal agents have been built for release in Q4 2026.

issues: 'The published abstract itself does not mention counter-offers' is true of the abstract but the normative text settles the point. Cl. 5.3.1 gives the entity three responses: accept, 'Respond to the individual with a single alternative set of terms from the structured and bounded list', or reject. Cl. 5.2.2 caps it: 'There shall be no negotiation beyond the single choice by either party.' The DPV community group's 'single counter-offer' is therefore the standard's own rule, not only a reading of a draft. Informative Annex A walks through one counter-offer and says IEEE 7012 'does not permit more than 1 round of negotiation'.

'The person's agent can record the refusal' understates the rule. Recording is mandatory: 'The recorder shall record rejected agreements including date, time, and entity refusing the offer' (cl. 5.2.4), and 'If an agreement is not reached, a record shall be generated to document rejection' (cl. 5.3.1).
Cl. 5.3.1(c) adds a rule this record did not carry: a rejecting entity 'cannot bar an individual from utilizing free or public information or services'.

fieldFixes.summary: The person's agent proposes the person's preferred agreement (cl. 5.4). The organisation's agent may accept it, reject it, or 'Respond to the individual with a single alternative set of terms from the structured and bounded list' (cl. 5.3.1), and 'There shall be no negotiation beyond the single choice by either party' (cl. 5.2.2). The abstract puts party-to-party negotiation over the terms of any agreement out of scope. So the permitted moves are a choice among roster agreements, not bargaining over their terms. A refusal must be recorded, with date, time and the refusing entity (cl. 5.2.4). A rejecting entity 'cannot bar an individual from utilizing free or public information or services' (cl. 5.3.1). The informative Annex A walks through one counter-offer and says the standard 'does not permit more than 1 round of negotiation'. The W3C DPV community group's P7012 extension (v2.1, March 2025, repeated in v2.2, August 2025) says the same. Doc Searls (January 2026) says a person may offer 'a first and second choice of agreement, but no more than that', and MyData Global says organisations may accept or propose an alternative from the same list.

fieldFixes.correction: The standard names no header, blockchain or identity system. Its clauses say only that its operation 'depends on the Internet Protocol Suite, especially TCP/IP, and HTTP' (cl. 1.3), and that both agents sign 'using any standard method agreed upon for that purpose' (cl. 5.4.2). A party may be identified by public keys, an email address or a pseudonym, 'so long as an IP address is present' (cl. 5.4.5). The abstract adds that agents may use 'any protocol that serves the purpose'. What the standard does require is an agreement signed electronically by both sides, identical and immutable copies kept by each, and a record with set minimum contents (terms, date, time stamp, identifiers and a unique contract ID). The record's format and storage are left open. The HTTP-header encoding in Annex A.2 is an informative example. Plug-ins, a transparency log and Doc Searls's 'MyTerms Agreement Record' are implementation ideas, not requirements. Searls, the working-group chair, says MyTerms should not depend on a universal identity system.

The functions are prescribed, though: cl. 5.2.1.1 says the individual's agent 'shall be constructed by including the components' set out after it (the chooser and proposer, cl. 5.2.1.2-5.2.1.3), and cl. 5.2.4-5.2.5 add recorder and auditor functions. --check FOUND 2026-09-23.

issues: The value (5) is right for MyTerms' launch roster, but it is not a figure in the standard, and the site's hero stat attributes it to 'IEEE 7012 / MyTerms'. IEEE 7012 sets no number. Cl. 4.1 says only 'There should also be as few agreements as possible'. Its informative Annex A (Table A.1) lists 13 sample agreements (ten SD-BASE variants plus PDC-INTENT, PDC-AI and PDC-GOOD), of which the five are a subset. Five at launch plus the FAQ's '8 more in the pipeline' also makes 13. The informative use case in Annex B.2 imagines 'a range of 10 standard agreements' (FOUND). The notes are extended, and a prose fix to the hero stat is filed.

fieldFixes.notes: Announced roster: SD-BASE, SD-BASE-DP, PDC-AI, PDC-GOOD, PDC-INTENT, with '8 more in the pipeline'. MyTerms says it will run these for up to six months for market feedback, then update them before a 'full market launch'. The launch event was held 28 January 2026 in London. As of their last 2026 updates, the myterms.info pages still describe the five in the future tense, and none of them links to published agreement texts. The number is MyTerms', not the standard's. IEEE 7012 sets no number of agreements; cl. 4.1 says only that there 'should' be 'as few agreements as possible'. Its informative Annex A (Table A.1) lists 13 sample agreements: SD-BASE, SD-BASE-DP, SD-BASE-A, SD-BASE-A-DP, SD-BASE-AT, SD-BASE-AT-DP, SD-BASE-ATP, SD-BASE-ATP-DP, SD-BASE-ATP-S3P, SD-BASE-ATP-S3P-DP, PDC-INTENT, PDC-AI and PDC-GOOD. The launch five are a subset, and five plus the eight in the pipeline also makes 13.

addSources.title: IEEE Std 7012-2025, IEEE Standard for Machine Readable Personal Privacy Terms, cl. 4.1 Form and content
addSources.quote: There should also be as few agreements as possible, to make choosing one as easy as possible for persons and their agents as first parties
addSources.note: Normative clause, recommendation ('should'). The standard sets no number of agreements; it asks for as few as possible. --check FOUND 2026-09-23.
